questions.lead: Describe, with examples, how using microprocessor-controlled devices in the home can affect the health and fitness of users.
points: Negative (less physical activity/sedentary, with example) and positive (more time/encouragement to exercise, fitness trackers) effects, balanced.
questions.tip: Worth 6 marks. Examiners reward distinct, specific points. Aim for at least 6 clearly different statements rather than one long sentence.
questions.model: Negative effects: labour-saving devices (washing machines, robot vacuum cleaners) mean people do less physical activity and can become less fit; more time on microprocessor entertainment devices encourages a sedentary, less healthy lifestyle. questions.lead: Discuss the positive and negative effects of using microprocessor-controlled devices in transport safety.
points: Positive (warns driver/faster reaction/fewer accidents) and negative (over-reliance/complacency; failure/hacking; cost). Balance for full marks.
questions.tip: High-tariff question (6 marks). Spread your answer across the sub-parts and use precise ICT keywords — vague answers lose easy marks here.
questions.model: Positive: the devices can warn the driver of hazards or speed limits, react faster than a human, and so help to reduce accidents and improve safety. Negative: the driver may rely on them too much and become complacent or less skilled; the system could fail or be hacked, giving wrong information; and the technology is expensive to fit and maintain. Overall they improve safety but should support, not replace, an attentive driver.

questions.lead: Discuss the positive and negative effects of using microprocessor-controlled devices in autonomous vehicles.
points: Positive (fewer accidents; mobility for elderly/disabled; smoother traffic; free time) and negative (failure/hacking; cost; job losses; legal/trust). Balance for full marks.
questions.tip: 6 marks = about 6 separate points. Make every sentence earn its own mark — don't reword the same idea twice.
questions.model: Positive: removing human error could reduce accidents; they can help elderly or disabled people travel; they can smooth traffic flow and let the occupant do other things. Negative: a software failure or hacking could be dangerous; they are expensive; they could cause job losses for professional drivers; and there are unresolved legal questions over who is responsible in a crash, plus public trust issues. Overall they offer real safety and convenience benefits but raise serious reliability, cost and responsibility concerns.
